title: Willow grades and varieties
subtitle: Understanding buff, brown, white, and green willow for basketry
excerpt: Basketry willow comes in four main grades, each handling and soaking differently. Each grade handles and soaks differently, suiting different projects. This guide explains what the grades are, how they are produced, which projects suit each, and how to source them in the UK.
sourceNotes: Twining, Basketwork for Beginners (1920) for the willow grade descriptions; Cassell's Cyclopaedia of Mechanics vol. III (1885) for the processing method comparison.

glossaryTerms.definition: Willow boiled in water to fix a warm tan colour, then stripped. The most widely available grade; good for all basket types.
Willow stripped of bark while still fresh, before any processing. Pale cream colour, fine finish, more expensive than buff.
Willow dried with bark on. The rough exterior makes it suitable for rustic field baskets but not fine work. Cheapest grade.
Freshly cut willow, used immediately without drying. Very flexible but available only in season and spoils quickly.

content.text: How basketry willow is processed determines how it handles and how long it soaks before use. The dried grades,
, behave differently from the undried grades,

. All four come from different points in the harvest and processing chain. Understanding the differences means buying the right grade for a project rather than discovering midway through that the basket needs a two-day soak you hadn't planned for.

Buff is the standard grade. The rods are harvested in winter, bundled, and boiled in open tanks for several hours. Boiling gelatinises the bark tannins, which fixes a warm tan colour through the bark and into the surface of the rod. The bark is then stripped while the rods are still hot, leaving a smooth, uniformly coloured rod. Buff willow soaks overnight (8, 12 hours) and should rest wrapped in a damp cloth for at least 30 minutes before working. It is the most forgiving grade: tolerates slight over-soaking and the colour is consistent.

Brown willow is dried with the bark intact. The bark is rough and provides a naturally rustic appearance. Brown willow requires a longer soak, 24, 48 hours, because the bark slows moisture absorption. When fully soaked it is workable, but less pliable than buff or white. Suited to field baskets, log baskets, and any application where a rough exterior is acceptable. Cheaper than buff; more likely to snap if under-soaked.

White willow is stripped fresh, immediately after harvest, while the sap is still running and the bark slips easily. Stripping while fresh produces the palest possible rod, nearly cream. White willow is dried after stripping and then soaks quickly before use (4, 6 hours). It gives the finest finished surface of any grade and is the choice for display baskets and any piece where colour matters. More expensive than buff. Willow for the Royal Maundy money and traditional English swill baskets is white.

Green willow is freshly cut and used directly. No soaking is needed because it is already saturated with moisture. It is the most flexible grade and can be worked at scales that would snap buff. Available only from March to September (outside of frost); it must be worked within a week of cutting as it dries out quickly once cut and starts to lose pliability. Traditionally used for stake-and-strand hurdle work, living willow structures, and large garden baskets. Not available from craft suppliers, sourced from coppice or grown specifically.

Within buff willow, the main UK varieties: Black Maul (fine rods for small and medium baskets), Dicky Meadows (very fine rods for detailed work), and viminalis (thick rods for bases). Craft suppliers sell by rod size within each grade rather than by named variety.
P.H. Coate & Son, Somerset: the main UK supplier of all grades. Sells in bolts (standard bundles) by grade and size. Most craft suppliers source from Coate.
The Basketmakers' Association: lists growers and suppliers, and has secondhand bolts from members.
Craft suppliers: buff willow in mixed sizes is the most available; white is special-order from most. Brown is less common in small quantities.
